extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, writing students, and general readers interested in screenwriting and story structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on Blake Snyder's Save the Cat method for structuring screenplays and stories, including the 15-beat Beat Sheet (BS2), the expanded 40-beat Board, genre taxonomy, workshops, and software tools. Useful for writers mapping beats, pacing, and story rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the Cat! moment (title concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: The title 'Save the Cat!' describes a decisive moment when the protagonist demonstrates that they are worth rooting for: "It's the scene where we [first] meet the hero". This moment gains audience favor and investment in the main character's well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In Frequency the hero's early action (jumping into a manhole to save workers) establishes likability and audience investment. Anti-pattern: prioritizing 'cool' or sex appeal over likability (cited example: Lara Croft sequel), which can reduce audience rooting interest and hurt box office performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blake Snyder Beat Sheet (BS2) — 15 essential beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Snyder's Beat Sheet (BS2) lays out 15 essential 'beats' or plot points that he asserts all stories should contain. He emphasizes the importance of structure and prescribes where key beats should occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beats are mapped to screenplay pages (pages ≈ minutes), producing a by-the-minute pattern for screenwriting. This prescriptive mapping is central to Snyder's approach and is used to evaluate pacing and plot placement. Critics argue this minute-by-minute guidance can encourage formulaic scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded 40 beats / The Board
rubrics_metrics.description: Snyder expanded the 15 beats into 40 beats laid out on 'The Board', which is divided into 4 rows representing the 1st Act, 1st half of the 2nd Act, 2nd half of the 2nd Act, and the 3rd Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board converts beats into 40 cards for a more detailed story structure and pacing map. This method is used in the Board Workshop and in Save the Cat software; it supports granular planning of quarter-by-quarter story development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten Save the Cat genres (genre taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Snyder introduced a taxonomy of 10 genres that distinguish how stories are structured (rather than just labeling type of movie). Examples include 'Monster in the House', 'Golden Fleece', and 'Buddy Love'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snyder argues traditional genre labels (romantic comedy, epic, biography) don't fully describe structural needs; his taxonomy is intended to guide beat placement and story mechanics. His follow-up book analyzed 50 films, identifying their Save the Cat genres and mapping them to the 15 beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page-to-minute beat timing (beat placement by screenplay page)
rubrics_metrics.description: Snyder's method maps specific beats to particular screenplay pages, treating screenplay pages as minutes of film and prescribing where beats should occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precise timing is used to judge pacing and whether a screenplay follows the recommended rhythm. It has drawn criticism for promoting formulaic, minute-by-minute writing; commentary debates whether the method caused industry trends or merely described them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat Sheet Workshop methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: An instructional workshop format: The Beat Sheet Workshop helps participants create the 15 beats (core structure) before writing; The Board Workshop expands those beats into 40 cards for detailed structuring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshops are taught in-person and online (including by 'Master Cats' trained by Snyder) and are intended to guide writers through the practical application of the Beat Sheet and Board. They are used by writers, filmmakers, executives, and in university settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the Cat software and templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Companion story-structure software that places Snyder's Beat Sheet and Board on desktop, phone, or tablet; later versions include templates for novelists and television writers and integration with Final Draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software supports import/export with script programs, mobile apps, and provides templates to apply Snyder's beats and board digitally. It operationalizes the Beat Sheet/Board for planning and editing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism: formulaic outcome risk
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring critique of Snyder's approach is that specifying beat locations and page numbers encourages formulaic screenplays and a perceived Hollywood formulaic trend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical sources (e.g., New York Times, Slate) argue that minute-by-minute prescriptions can stifle originality; reviewers debate whether Snyder popularized an existing trend or reflected prevailing industry patterns. Writers should weigh structural guidance against risks of over-formulaic storytelling.
